questionText: Who established the first formal psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879?
explanation: Wilhelm Wundt set up the first experimental psychology laboratory at Leipzig, Germany, in 1879, marking psychology's birth as a science.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: The word 'psychology' is derived from the Greek words 'psyche' and 'logos'. What do they mean?
explanation: Psyche means soul (or mind) and logos means study or discourse, so psychology originally meant the study of the soul.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Which school of psychology was founded by Sigmund Freud?
explanation: Freud founded psychoanalysis, which emphasises the role of the unconscious mind in shaping behaviour.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Which American psychologist is associated with functionalism and wrote 'The Principles of Psychology'?
explanation: William James led functionalism, focusing on how mental processes help organisms adapt, and wrote 'The Principles of Psychology' (1890).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Which method did structuralists such as Titchener mainly use to analyse the elements of conscious experience?
explanation: Structuralists trained observers to introspect, that is, to report their own sensations and feelings systematically.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: John B. Watson argued that psychology should study only what?
explanation: Watson's behaviourism rejected mental states as unscientific and limited psychology to observable, measurable behaviour.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Which idea best summarises Gestalt psychology?

options.text: Behaviour is shaped only by reinforcement
The mind is made of basic sensory elements
The whole is different from the sum of its parts

explanation: Gestalt psychologists like Wertheimer held that we perceive organised wholes rather than isolated elements.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Which pair of psychologists is most closely associated with the humanistic perspective?

options.text: Ivan Pavlov and B. F. Skinner

explanation: Maslow and Rogers emphasised free will, personal growth and self-actualisation, forming the humanistic 'third force'.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: The cognitive perspective in psychology mainly focuses on which of the following?

options.text: Mental processes such as thinking, memory and problem solving

explanation: Cognitive psychology studies how people acquire, process and store information.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Which definition best reflects the modern view of psychology?

options.text: The scientific study of behaviour and mental processes
The study of observable behaviour alone

explanation: Modern psychology combines the study of overt behaviour with internal mental processes, using scientific methods.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Where was the first department of experimental psychology in India established in 1915?
explanation: The University of Calcutta started India's first experimental psychology department in 1915, with N. N. Sengupta playing a key role.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Why was introspection criticised as a scientific method?

options.text: It relied too heavily on animal experiments
Reports were subjective and could not be independently verified

explanation: Different observers gave different reports of the same stimulus, and private experience could not be checked by others.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Ivan Pavlov's work on salivation in dogs contributed which concept to behaviourism?
explanation: Pavlov showed that a neutral stimulus paired with food could come to elicit salivation, the basis of classical conditioning.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Story of Psychology

questionText: Which branch of psychology deals with the assessment and treatment of psychological disorders?
explanation: Clinical psychologists assess, diagnose and treat psychological disorders using therapy and testing.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Which branch applies psychological principles to teaching and learning in schools?
explanation: Educational psychology studies how students learn and how teaching can be made more effective.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Employee selection, training and workplace motivation are studied mainly in which branch?
explanation: I-O psychology applies psychology to the workplace, including recruitment, training and productivity.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: A psychologist helping athletes manage performance anxiety before a match is working in which field?
explanation: Sports psychology deals with mental factors such as motivation, focus and anxiety that affect athletic performance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Evaluating the reliability of eyewitness testimony in a court case falls under which branch?
explanation: Forensic psychology applies psychology to the legal and criminal justice system, including eyewitness accounts.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Which branch studies how psychological factors such as lifestyle and stress influence physical illness?
explanation: Health psychology examines the links between behaviour, psychological factors and physical health.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Which branch studies changes in a person from conception through old age?
explanation: Developmental psychology studies physical, cognitive and social changes across the life span.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Studying how the presence of others influences conformity and attitudes belongs to which branch?
explanation: Social psychology studies how individuals think, feel and behave in social situations.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: How does counselling psychology usually differ from clinical psychology?

options.text: It focuses mainly on everyday adjustment problems rather than severe disorders
It deals only with criminal offenders

explanation: Counsellors typically help people with career, family and adjustment issues, while clinical psychologists handle more severe disorders.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Research on how noise, crowding and pollution affect behaviour is part of which branch?
explanation: Environmental psychology studies the interaction between people and their physical surroundings.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Which branch studies the relationship between brain functioning and behaviour, often in people with brain injuries?
explanation: Neuropsychology links specific brain structures and damage to changes in cognition and behaviour.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes pure from applied branches of psychology?

options.text: Pure branches build basic theory, while applied branches use that knowledge to solve practical problems
Pure branches use experiments, while applied branches never use research
Pure branches study humans, while applied branches study only animals
Pure branches are practised only in hospitals

explanation: Pure (basic) branches like general psychology develop principles; applied branches like clinical or I-O psychology put them into practice.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Branches of Psychology

questionText: The organised set of beliefs a person holds about who they are is called what?
explanation: Self-concept is the overall picture or perception a person has of themselves.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: A person's overall evaluation of their own worth is known as what?
explanation: Self-esteem is the evaluative, value-based judgement of oneself as worthy or unworthy.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: Who developed the Johari Window model of self-awareness?
explanation: The Johari Window (1955) was named after its creators, Joseph Luft and Harry Ingham.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: According to Carl Rogers, the person one would like to be is called the what?
explanation: Rogers distinguished the real self (who we are) from the ideal self (who we wish to be).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: In the Johari Window, information known to both oneself and others belongs to which area?
explanation: The open (arena) quadrant contains traits and facts known to the self and to others.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: A friend points out that you interrupt people often, which you had never noticed. This trait was in which Johari area?
explanation: The blind area contains things others know about us that we ourselves are unaware of.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: Private fears you know about but deliberately keep from others belong to which Johari area?
explanation: The hidden (facade) area contains what we know about ourselves but do not disclose.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: William James distinguished the self as knower from the self as known. What did he call these?
explanation: James described the 'I' as the subjective knower and the 'Me' as the self that is known or observed.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: Charles Cooley's 'looking-glass self' suggests that self-concept develops mainly through what?

options.text: How we imagine others see and judge us

explanation: Cooley proposed that we form our self-image by reflecting on how others perceive and evaluate us.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: According to Rogers, a large gap between the real self and the ideal self leads to what?
explanation: Rogers held that incongruence between real and ideal self produces tension and anxiety, while congruence supports well-being.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: Albert Bandura defined self-efficacy as what?

options.text: The tendency to compare oneself with others
Belief in one's ability to succeed in a specific task or situation

explanation: Self-efficacy is a task-specific belief in one's capability, which influences effort and persistence.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: Which change in the Johari Window is generally encouraged for healthy relationships?

options.text: Enlarging the open area through self-disclosure and feedback
Enlarging the hidden area by sharing less
Enlarging the blind area by avoiding feedback
Keeping all four areas equal in size

explanation: Self-disclosure shrinks the hidden area and seeking feedback shrinks the blind area, expanding the open area.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: Leon Festinger's social comparison theory states that people evaluate themselves by doing what?

options.text: Looking only at their past achievements
Comparing their abilities and opinions with those of others

explanation: Festinger proposed that, lacking objective standards, people judge themselves by comparison with others.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Self

questionText: When does the prenatal period of development begin?

options.text: At the end of the first month
When the heart begins to beat

explanation: The prenatal period runs from conception (fertilisation) to birth.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: Which psychologist proposed four stages of cognitive development in children?
explanation: Piaget proposed the sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational stages.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: The biological process of sexual maturation that marks the start of adolescence is called what?
explanation: Puberty involves hormonal changes and development of secondary sexual characteristics.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: Which stage of development covers roughly the first two years after birth?
explanation: Infancy spans from birth to about two years and is marked by rapid physical and motor growth.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: Object permanence develops during which Piagetian stage?
explanation: During the sensorimotor stage (0-2 years) infants learn that objects continue to exist when out of sight.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: A four-year-old assumes everyone sees the same view she does. Piaget called this what?
explanation: Egocentrism, the inability to take another's perspective, is typical of the preoperational stage.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: Understanding that the amount of water stays the same when poured into a taller glass is called what?
explanation: Conservation is mastered in the concrete operational stage (about 7-11 years).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: Abstract and hypothetical-deductive reasoning first appears in which stage?
explanation: From about age 11-12, adolescents can reason about abstract ideas and hypothetical possibilities.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: According to Erikson, the main psychosocial crisis of adolescence is what?
explanation: Erikson held that adolescents must form a stable sense of identity or face role confusion.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: Which is the correct order of the prenatal periods?
explanation: The germinal period (first two weeks) is followed by the embryonic (to about 8 weeks) and then the foetal period until birth.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: A baby starts walking at about the same age regardless of training. This mainly shows the role of what?
explanation: Maturation is the biologically programmed unfolding of abilities, largely independent of practice.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: Consistent, responsive caregiving during infancy helps resolve which Eriksonian crisis?
explanation: In the first stage, reliable care leads infants to develop basic trust in the world.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Human Development

questionText: According to the WHO, health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely what?

options.text: The absence of disease or infirmity

explanation: The WHO definition stresses positive well-being across physical, mental and social domains.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Who is widely regarded as the founder of positive psychology?
explanation: Martin Seligman promoted positive psychology in 1998, focusing on strengths and well-being.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Defining behaviour as abnormal because it is rare or far from the average uses which criterion?
explanation: The statistical criterion treats behaviour that deviates greatly from the population average as abnormal.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Judging behaviour as abnormal because it violates the accepted rules of a society uses which criterion?
explanation: The social norm criterion compares behaviour against the expectations of a given society.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Behaviour that prevents a person from carrying out daily activities such as work or study is described as what?
explanation: The maladaptiveness criterion focuses on whether behaviour interferes with everyday functioning.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Marie Jahoda's view of mental health emphasised which idea?

options.text: Positive features such as self-acceptance, growth and environmental mastery

explanation: Jahoda described positive mental health in terms of qualities like autonomy, accurate perception and self-acceptance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: The ability to bounce back and adapt well after adversity is called what?
explanation: Resilience is the capacity to recover from difficulties and adapt positively.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Which statement about normality is most accurate?

options.text: Normal people never experience negative emotions
Normality and abnormality lie on a continuum rather than being strict opposites
Normality is identical in every culture
Any unusual behaviour is a disorder

explanation: Most psychologists see behaviour as varying by degree along a continuum from healthy to unhealthy functioning.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Why is the statistical criterion alone an inadequate definition of abnormality?

options.text: It treats all common behaviours as disorders
Some rare traits, such as exceptional giftedness, are desirable rather than abnormal
It depends entirely on personal distress

explanation: Statistical rarity does not distinguish between desirable and undesirable deviations.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: What is a major limitation of the social norm criterion of abnormality?

options.text: Norms differ across cultures and change over time

explanation: Because norms are culture- and era-specific, the same behaviour may be judged normal in one setting and abnormal in another.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: In Seligman's PERMA model of well-being, what does the letter 'M' stand for?
explanation: PERMA stands for Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning and Accomplishment.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Why is personal distress alone not sufficient as a criterion of abnormality?

options.text: Distress can never be reported by individuals
Some people with serious problems feel no distress, while distress is normal after events like bereavement
Distress is only a physical symptom
Distress always indicates a statistical rarity

explanation: Distress can be a normal reaction to life events, and some disturbed behaviour occurs without distress to the person.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Healthy Me - Normal Me

questionText: Who proposed the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) model of stress?
explanation: Endocrinologist Hans Selye described the body's three-stage response to prolonged stress.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: Positive stress that motivates a person and improves performance is called what?
explanation: Eustress is beneficial stress, such as the excitement before an important performance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: Harmful stress that leads to anxiety and reduced performance is called what?
explanation: Distress is negative stress that overwhelms coping resources and impairs functioning.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: An event or situation that triggers a stress response is known as what?
explanation: A stressor is any internal or external demand perceived as challenging or threatening.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: What is the correct sequence of stages in Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome?
explanation: The body first reacts with alarm, then tries to adapt (resistance), and finally becomes depleted (exhaustion).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: The sudden activation of the sympathetic nervous system when a stressor appears occurs in which GAS stage?
explanation: In the alarm reaction the body mobilises for fight or flight, raising heart rate and releasing stress hormones.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: In Lazarus's model, deciding whether an event is threatening or irrelevant is called what?
explanation: Primary appraisal evaluates the significance of an event for one's well-being.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: Assessing whether one has the resources to cope with a stressor is called what?
explanation: Secondary appraisal evaluates one's coping abilities and resources for handling the stressor.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: Making a study timetable to deal with exam pressure is an example of which coping style?
explanation: Problem-focused coping tackles the source of stress directly by planning and taking action.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: A student wants to join a prestigious college but dreads its high fees. This is which type of conflict?
explanation: Approach-avoidance conflict involves a single goal with both attractive and unattractive features.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: Having to choose between two unpleasant options, such as cleaning the house or doing a disliked chore, is which conflict?
explanation: Avoidance-avoidance conflict arises when one must choose between two undesirable alternatives.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: According to Selye, why does prolonged exposure to stress increase vulnerability to illness?

options.text: The alarm stage permanently strengthens immunity
Bodily resources become depleted in the exhaustion stage
Stress affects only thoughts, not the body

explanation: Long-term stress drains physiological reserves, weakening immunity and raising the risk of disease.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: Which personality pattern, marked by time urgency, competitiveness and hostility, has been linked to heart disease?
explanation: Friedman and Rosenman linked the Type A pattern, especially its hostility component, to coronary heart disease.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Stress

questionText: What is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system?
explanation: Neurons are specialised cells that receive, process and transmit information.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: The central nervous system consists of which structures?
explanation: The CNS comprises the brain and spinal cord; all other nerves form the peripheral nervous system.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Which part of a neuron mainly receives incoming signals from other neurons?
explanation: Dendrites are branching extensions that receive messages and carry them toward the cell body.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and smooth voluntary movement?
explanation: The cerebellum ('little brain') coordinates posture, balance and fine motor movement.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: What is the main function of the myelin sheath?

options.text: To receive signals from other neurons
To speed up transmission of nerve impulses along the axon

explanation: Myelin insulates the axon so impulses jump between nodes, greatly increasing conduction speed.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: How is a message usually passed from one neuron to the next across a synapse?

options.text: By chemical neurotransmitters released into the synaptic gap
By direct physical fusion of the two neurons
By hormones from the pituitary gland

explanation: Neurotransmitters released from axon terminals cross the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the next neuron.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Which brain structure controls vital functions such as breathing and heart rate?
explanation: The medulla in the brainstem regulates automatic life-sustaining functions.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Which division of the autonomic nervous system prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
explanation: The sympathetic division increases heart rate and energy mobilisation during emergencies.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Which lobe of the cerebral cortex is primarily responsible for processing visual information?
explanation: The occipital lobe at the back of the brain contains the primary visual cortex.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Damage to Broca's area in the left frontal lobe most typically affects what?
explanation: Broca's area is involved in producing fluent speech; damage leads to slow, effortful speech.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Which structure regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature and controls the pituitary gland?
explanation: The hypothalamus maintains homeostasis and links the nervous system to the endocrine system.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: What is the function of the corpus callosum?

options.text: It relays sensory information to the cortex
It connects the two cerebral hemispheres and allows them to communicate

explanation: The corpus callosum is a thick band of nerve fibres linking the left and right hemispheres.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: Why can you pull your hand away from a hot object before you consciously feel pain?

options.text: The cerebellum interprets pain faster than the cortex
Hormones carry the signal directly to the muscles
The parasympathetic system blocks pain signals
The reflex arc is processed in the spinal cord without first going to the brain

explanation: In a reflex arc, sensory neurons connect via interneurons in the spinal cord to motor neurons, producing a rapid response.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Nervous System

questionText: What are the three basic processes of memory, in order?
explanation: Information must first be encoded, then stored, and later retrieved when needed.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: According to George Miller, the capacity of short-term memory is about how many items?
explanation: Miller's 'magical number seven, plus or minus two' describes the limited capacity of short-term memory.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: Who first plotted the 'forgetting curve' using nonsense syllables?
explanation: Ebbinghaus showed that forgetting is rapid at first and then levels off over time.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: Who proposed the multi-store (three-store) model of memory?
explanation: Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) described sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: Which memory store holds a very brief, large-capacity record of incoming sensory information?
explanation: Sensory memory holds information for a fraction of a second to a few seconds before it fades or is attended to.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: Answering a multiple-choice question rather than a fill-in-the-blank question mainly involves which retrieval method?
explanation: Recognition requires identifying previously learned material among options, which is usually easier than recall.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: Remembering your last birthday celebration is an example of which type of memory?
explanation: Tulving defined episodic memory as memory for personally experienced events tied to time and place.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: Knowing how to ride a bicycle is stored as which type of memory?
explanation: Procedural memory stores skills and habits that are performed without conscious recollection.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: You keep writing your old phone number when asked for your new one. This illustrates what?
explanation: In proactive interference, old learning disrupts the recall of newer information.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: After learning French, a student finds it harder to recall Spanish learned earlier. This is an example of what?
explanation: In retroactive interference, new learning disrupts the recall of previously learned information.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: Better recall of the first and last items in a list than the middle items is known as what?
explanation: The serial position effect combines the primacy effect (early items) and the recency effect (final items).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory

questionText: According to Craik and Lockhart, which kind of processing leads to the most durable memories?
explanation: The levels of processing approach holds that analysing meaning produces stronger, longer-lasting memory traces.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Memory
